title: Conserved synaptic modifications by humanized tau through diverse isoform- and mutation-specific intracellular interactions
authors: Nickerson, E.; Pomeroy-Tuck, J.; Pratt, S.; Rodriguez, C.; Zhao, T.; Stodola, T.; Hoffman, B.; Maser, R.; Bloss, E.
abstract: Mutations in the microtubule-binding protein tau are considered causal for a diverse group of neurodegenerative diseases collectively referred to as primary tauopathies. Specific tauopathies are associated with different mutations, distinct tau isoforms, manifest in unique cellular and circuit-wide patterns of degeneration, and present with specific clinical symptoms and trajectories. The mechanisms that link variations in the primary tau protein structure to distinct forms of neural circuit dysfunction remain largely unknown. Here, we created an orthogonal viral resource to systematically examine the impact of expressing humanized tau isoforms harboring different disease-relevant mutations in excitatory pyramidal cells from the mouse prelimbic cortex. We used these reagents to show that expression of mutant humanized tau (hTau) as either of two isoforms produced very similar patterns of circuit-specific synaptic disconnection on cortical projection neurons. However, mass spectrometry revealed that the interactomes of these different tau species varied markedly as functions of isoform, mutation, and subcellular location. We validated the functional relevance of increased hTau interactions with mitochondrial proteins in induced neurons differentiated from Ngn2-iPSCs expressing different hTau constructs. These results suggest different disease-relevant hTau proteins likely use distinct mechanisms to drive a highly stereotyped form of synapse loss in cortical neurons.

title: Serial dependence carries the action that produced the previous report
authors: Qu, C.; Naeve, C.; Shi, Z.
abstract: Serial dependence pulls current judgments toward the recent past, but what is carried forward is debated: the previous stimulus, the previous decision, or something about the report itself. Three magnitude-reproduction experiments separated these sources. Participants viewed dot arrays that varied independently in duration and numerosity, then reproduced the cued dimension by holding a key while a display accumulated, so that both magnitudes were produced through the same action. A response-history model partitioned the attraction into previous-stimulus and previous-response paths. The previous response predicted cross-dimensional attraction after controlling for the previous and current stimuli: a numerosity report biased the next duration judgment and vice versa (Experiment 1), also when each task used its own response key (Experiment 2). A task switch weakened this carryover without abolishing it. Experiment 3 randomized, trial by trial, whether a reported number required a long or a short key hold. The influence of a previous number on the next duration judgment changed with this mapping, showing that reported value alone did not account for carryover. Conventional stimulus-based measures showed none of this cross-task history. Serial dependence can therefore carry the trace of the action through which a previous judgment was expressed, bounded but not gated by task context.

title: Mitochondria-Coupled Hitchhiking Drives Vimentin Intermediate Filament Transport
authors: Renganathan, B.; Moore, A. S.; Adam, S. A.; Lippincott-Schwartz, J.; Gelfand, V. I.
abstract: Vimentin intermediate filaments (VIFs) undergo active microtubule-dependent transport throughout the cell, with trajectories resembling those of motor-driven organelles, yet our recent work showed that only a small subset of VIFs lies close to microtubules. How VIFs engage the microtubule-based transport machinery, and whether additional transport routes contribute, remain unresolved. We hypothesized that VIFs move indirectly, by hitchhiking on motile organelles, and tested this using mitochondria. Live imaging showed mitochondria and adjacent VIFs moving together, and volume electron microscopy revealed VIFs closely following mitochondrial surfaces at sites distinct from microtubule contacts. Depleting the mitochondrial motor adaptor TRAK1 to inhibit anterograde mitochondrial transport shifted both mitochondria and VIFs toward the nucleus. Driving mitochondria toward the cell periphery with a tailless kinesin-1 in cells lacking endogenous kinesin-1, or toward the cell center with a minus-end-directed motor, redistributed a subset of VIFs in the same direction. Thus, VIF transport to a large extend is accomplished by hitchhiking on motile mitochondria.

title: Sex-specific bone marrow populations regulate skeletal phenotype and identify CD74-marked osteoclast precursor subsets
authors: Koroth, J.; Karkache, I. Y.; Vu, E. K.; Manser, J. C.; Mitchell, S.; Shimak, M. J.; Robertson, N.; Patterson, E.; Kiraguri, S.; Mansky, K. M.; Bradley, E.
abstract: While there are clear differences in bone accrual and maintenance between men and women due to hormonal regulation, the potential cell-intrinsic factors governing this difference are poorly understood. To investigate this, we performed bone marrow transplantation assays using male or female bone marrow transplantation into male hosts. Micro-CT analyses of lethally irradiated 8-week-old male mice transplanted with female bone marrow exhibited increased vertebral body trabecular and cortical bone mass. To identify cell types mediating these effects, we performed comparative single cell sequencing analyses and identified several CD11B+CD74+ myeloid cell clusters. Male donor BM chimeric mice had a higher proportion of Cd74-expressing clusters compared to female donor BM chimeric mice. We confirmed that males have greater numbers of bone marrow-resident CD11B+CD74+ cells under physiological conditions. Elevated expression of X-linked genes Tlr7 and Kdm6a marked a population of CD11B+CD74+ cells. Lastly, we show that female CD11B+CD74+ cells exhibit diminished osteoclastogenesis. These findings demonstrate that male and female bone marrow-resident cells have cell-intrinsic differences that regulate bone mass and that CD74 marks a subset of osteoclast precursor-enriched myeloid populations.

title: Novel Regulators of Sugar-dependent Food Consumption in Drosophila melanogaster
authors: Opoola, M. A.; Fitzgerald, L.; Ahmed, S.; Wright, M.; Alli, S.; Wright, N.; Hwangbo, D.-S.
abstract: Diet and genetic background interact to influence food consumption, yet the genetic basis of diet-dependent feeding behavior remains poorly understood. Here, we used genome-wide association analysis (GWAS) to investigate the genetic regulation of sugar-dependent food consumption in Drosophila melanogaster. Food intake was quantified in 176 lines of the Drosophila Genetic Reference Panel (DGRP) using the Con-Ex (Consumption-Excretion) assay on low- and high-sugar foods. Flies showed compensatory feeding, consuming more low-sugar food than high-sugar food, and this behavior was largely maintained across genotypes. Additionally, the magnitude and overall consumption varied several-fold among lines, with broad-sense heritability of 0.53 to 0.66 across sexes and diets. Association analysis across six sex- and diet-specific phenotypes identified 161 variants mapping to 118 candidate genes, which shared almost no loci between dietary conditions, indicating that consumption on the two foods is largely under separate genetic control. RNAi knockdown of candidate genes identified CG42673 and Tmtc2, whose knockdown increased consumption across sexes and diets and was reproduced in independent experiments. Together, these findings show that natural genetic variation contributes substantially to diet-dependent feeding and identify candidate regulators of sugar-based food consumption in Drosophila.

title: Actin pool controls the scaling of dynamic actin networks
authors: Cantat, A.; Guerin, C.; Morel, N.; Vianay, B.; Mogilner, A.; Thery, M.; Blanchoin, L.; Colin, A.
abstract: Scaling is a fundamental property of living systems, allowing cells to match the size of their internal components to their volume. The size and shape of cells depend largely on the actin cytoskeleton, whose dynamic self-assembling structures are central to this adaptation. Yet how they self-assemble in a volume-dependent manner remains unresolved. To address this question, we used a biomimetic system consisting of beads propelled by actin polymerization in microwells of different volumes, which allowed us to work with a limited and defined number of components. This approach enabled the first reconstitution, from purified proteins, of dynamic cytoskeletal structures that adapt to the volume of their environment. The scalability of these structures depends on how strongly they deplete monomers from a shared pool, and tuning the disassembly rate is sufficient to shift their scaling regime. Scaling principles also hold for multiple competing structures, with greater competition imposing stronger constraints on the monomer pool. Together, these results establish a mechanistic framework in which a structure's capacity to adapt is set by how much it draws down shared resources as it grows, a principle that may extend to other intracellular structures that scale with the cells that build them.

title: Structural basis of ribosomal RNA repair by RtcB2
authors: Tian, Y.; Zhou, Q.; Yu, Q.; Huang, Y.; Zhang, W.; Huang, J.; Yu, T.; Zeng, F.
abstract: Ribotoxins disable ribosomes by cleaving ribosomal RNA, but how repair enzymes recognize and restore these damaged machines remains unclear. Here, we report three cryo-electron microscopy structures of the RNA ligase RtcB2 bound to damaged Escherichia coli 30S subunits. An extended interface stabilizes the ribosomal head and decoding-center scaffold while positioning the cleaved 3'-phosphate end within the catalytic pocket. Two structures contain enzyme-linked guanosine monophosphate, whereas the third captures its transfer to the RNA. RNA activation accompanies RtcB2 reorientation and entry of the 5'-hydroxyl-containing segment into an adjacent cleft. Comparisons with assembled ribosomes reveal structural barriers to substrate access. These structures connect recognition of a damaged ribosome to chemical activation of its RNA for repair.

title: Vorinostat Can Reduce an Ongoing Fibrosis and Preserve Key Liver Metabolic Functions by Selectively Altering Mesenchymal Cell Differentiation
abstract: Liver fibrosis is a major global cause of mortality that is driven by the activation of hepatic stellate cells (HSCs) into extracellular matrix (ECM)-producing myofibroblasts (MyoFs). The lack of predictive human in vitro models has severely hampered the discovery of targeted anti-fibrotic therapies. Here, we describe a human iPSC-derived hepatic micro-organoid (microHO) model, which labels collagen producing cells, to study liver fibrosis pathophysiology and screen drug candidates. We discovered that while multiple drugs prevented fibrosis when co-administered prophylactically with TGF{beta}1, only the FDA-approved pan-HDAC inhibitor Vorinostat (SAHA) successfully reduced an established, ongoing fibrosis and preserved life-sustaining liver metabolic functions in a fibrotic microenvironment, including ammonia detoxification and CYP3A4-mediated drug metabolism. To uncover its mechanism of action, we utilized single-cell RNA sequencing and CRISPR-Cas12a lineage tracing. We found that Vorinostat actively redirects HSC differentiation away from pro-fibrotic MyoFs and toward a distinct, fibrosis-suppressing mesenchymal inhibitory (MesInh) cell. By reversing TGF{beta}1-induced epigenetic silencing, Vorinostat opens condensed chromatin to rescue metabolic gene expression and generates anti-fibrotic effectors that neutralize ongoing TGF{beta}1 signaling. Given its distinct capacity to remodel mesenchymal cell fate and reverse epigenetic repression of metabolic genes at clinically achievable concentrations, Vorinostat represents a highly promising drug for repurposing as a therapeutic for advanced human liver fibrosis.

title: Nociceptive-evoked electroencephalography can predict inter-individual differences in high frequency induced sensitisation of central nociceptive pathways: A test-retest reliability study
authors: Mugglestone, S.; Hughes, S. W.; Ganis, G.
abstract: Evoked-EEG can capture changes in cortical responses during experimentally induced sensitised pain states. However, the test-retest reliability of such methods requires validation. The present study applied HFS across two identical sessions in the same individuals to assess the test-retest reliability of EEG dynamics evoked by a 128mN pin-prick stimulator and single-pulse electrical stimuli before and after HFS conditioning. The value of these features for reflecting individual differences in the development of hyperalgesia was also assessed. Results demonstrate poor-to-moderate test-retest reliability and relatively wide agreement at baseline for all features, with lateralised differences often present. This was further reduced when post-HFS changes were considered. -ERD assessed from contralateral central electrodes was significantly strengthened post-HFS for both electrical and pinprick stimuli, consistent with increased sensorimotor engagement in response to hyperalgesic and non-hyperalgesic stimuli. Notably, baseline -ERD was related to the subsequent time course of SHA development. Furthermore, whilst VP magnitude displayed a significant relationship with the general intensity of perceived pain, no specificity for SHA development was evident. Alternatively, {theta}-ERS captured a general habituation effect relative to variations in reported pain intensity between sessions for both stimuli modalities. These findings indicate that evoked EEG responses may be useful for investigating individual differences in the cortical processing of acute pain and the development time course of HFS-induced sensitivity yet may not possess sufficient test-retest reliability for interventional testing.

title: Automated Segmentation of the Hypothalamus: Associations of Age and Socioeconomic Status with Subunit Volumes in Cognitively Healthy Adults
abstract: Background: The hypothalamus regulates sleep-wake cycles, energy balance, and autonomic and neuroendocrine function, yet its small size and poorly contrasted boundaries have long hindered in vivo volumetry. Deep-learning segmentation now allows the hypothalamus to be divided into functionally meaningful subunits. We examined whether hypothalamic subunit volumes are associated with age and socioeconomic status (SES) in cognitively healthy adults. Methods: From the OASIS-1 cross-sectional dataset (n = 416, 18-96 years), 133 participants with a Clinical Dementia Rating of 0 and complete segmentation output were analysed (33-94 years). A FreeSurfer-based convolutional neural network, run on a cloud virtual machine, segmented five subunits per hemisphere. Volumes were normalised to estimated total intracranial volume (eTIV) and related to age and SES (Hollingshead index) using Pearson correlations with Benjamini-Hochberg false discovery rate (FDR) correction; partial correlations adjusted for sex (age) and for age and sex (SES) served as sensitivity analyses. Results: Older age was associated with lower normalised volume of the right posterior subunit (r = -.456, q < .001) and the left posterior subunit (r = -.274, q = .007); both associations persisted after adjustment for sex. Lower SES showed a trend towards larger left anterior-inferior volume (r = .242, uncorrected p = .005) that did not survive FDR correction (q = .053). Conclusions: Age-related volumetric differences in the healthy hypothalamus appear to be concentrated in its posterior portion, a region housing arousal-promoting circuitry. Automated subunit segmentation offers a scalable tool for studying the hypothalamus in ageing and in relation to environmental exposures; the cross-sectional associations reported here should not be interpreted as causal or as within-person change.

title: Gain Control of Peripheral Input by Core Brain Thermosensors Drives Drosophila Thermoregulation
authors: Lazopulo, S.; Zlatic, M.; Cardona, A.; Garrity, P.; Samuel, A. D. T.
abstract: Temperature affects all aspects of animal physiology, rendering thermoregulation critical for survival. In Drosophila larvae, well-established peripheral thermosensors detect temperature changes and mediate thermotaxis over a broad innocuous range, but how larvae seek a specific preferred body temperature within this range remains unknown. Here we show that core thermosensors in the brain (LPBT neurons) establish this setpoint by mediating warming-evoked turning at temperatures above it. LPBTs express the warmth-activated thermosensor TrpA1(A), but are not simply cell-autonomous thermosensors. Rather, sustained LPBT responses above setpoint require both peripheral thermosensory input and TRPA1-dependent thermosensing within LPBTs. TRPA1-dependent core thermosensing provides gain control that defines the homeostatic setpoint by tuning the behavioral weights of peripheral inputs. This new conception of thermal preference reveals parallels between Drosophila and mammalian thermoregulation.

title: Brain Decoding from a Deep Neural Network of Visual Memory Reveals the Maturation Trajectory of Memory Systems across Ages 3-7
authors: GUO, X.; Leong, Y. C.; Bainbridge, W. A.
abstract: Memories from the first four years of life are largely inaccessible by adulthood, yet these early experiences profoundly shape cognition throughout development. Understanding this phenomenon of infantile amnesia is critical for revealing the mechanisms of early memory development. Here, we developed a new content-based behavioral measure of memory that quantifies how closely children's memory patterns resemble those of adults, which we term the memory maturation score. Using a movie-watching fMRI dataset spanning age 3 to adulthood, we trained a cross-validated model on adults' movie-evoked brain activity to predict adult's propensity to remember each movie snippet, estimated by ResMem, a deep neural network trained to predict visual memorability. We then applied the model to each child's brain activity while viewing the same movie to assess their memory maturation (i.e., cross-decodability from adult patterns). Children exhibited adult-like neural patterns of memory around age 4, extending prior behavioral findings. Structural analyses showed that the volume of the left posterior hippocampus, but not age or total brain volume, significantly predicted children's memory maturation. Memory maturation around age 4 thus likely reflects age-related neural development of hippocampal memory systems, rather than an age increase itself. Functional searchlight analyses revealed a trajectory of memory maturation: the inferior temporal gyrus reflected mature memory-related processing from age 3 onward, the left posterior hippocampus by age 5, and higher-order regions involved in social-affective processing and multimodal integration by age 7. Together, these findings suggest that hippocampal maturation between ages 3 and 5 drives the maturation of memory patterns.

title: SafeLens: A Statistically Controlled Nonlinear Machine Learning Framework for Characterizing Hidden Dynamics in Event-Locked Neural Activity
authors: Minasi, C. B.; Hassan, U.; Cline, C. C.; Keller, C. J.
abstract: Machine learning has advanced rapidly over the past decade, yet event-locked neural activity is still analyzed predominantly with traditional statistics and linear models. While traditional linear methods provide computationally tractable statistical control for pre-selected features or trial-averaged waveforms, they miss subtle nonlinear and trial-varying neural dynamics. Nonlinear models can capture these complex patterns, but their feature reliance is opaque and notoriously difficult to threshold statistically. We introduce SafeLens (Searchlight Analysis of Fluctuation Events, Leveraging Extensive Null Sampling) to combine the power of nonlinear machine learning with the rigorous false-positive control of traditional statistical inference. At each position of a sliding window, a random forest learns to discriminate event-locked activity from interleaved resting-state neural activity using multiscale temporal derivatives. Randomized feature ablation inverts slope polarity in held-out trials to map the random forest models' reliance on specific rising versus falling excursions across the time-frequency space. SafeLens then establishes an empirical null by running the same pipeline on separate resting-state recordings, training forests to discriminate rest from rest. This empirical null translates each channel's complex nonlinear resting dynamics into a model-matched noise floor on the map's linear reliance scale, allowing a single threshold to control the family-wise error rate against the channel's own background structure rather than a summary statistic of its baseline. When we injected simulated cortico-cortical evoked potentials (CCEPs) into resting intracranial EEG recordings, SafeLens recovered ~2.5 times as many polarity-resolved deflections as trial-average thresholding and the closest data-driven method, maintaining its advantage under trial-to-trial variability while yielding ~5-11 times fewer false components, ~2-5 times lower mean boundary error, and superior single-trial latency tracking as a timing prior. In eight patients, CCEPs remained detectable above chance until 1,040 ms after stimulation, compared with 570 and 455 ms for those benchmarks. Together, these findings establish SafeLens as a novel solution for enabling nonlinear models to uncover subtle, trial-varying neural dynamics under strict statistical control.

title: Rapid Detection and Initial Treatment of Life-Threatening Subdural Hematoma in a Sheep Model
authors: Brody, D. L.; Dengler, B. A.; Angelo, J. P.; Blodgett, D. W.; Cohen, A. B.; Drewry, D. G.; Fitch, M. J.; Goonasekeram, N.; Januszkiewicz, A. J.; Knapp, T.; Kohler, B.; Mark, J.; McAdams, I. S.; Perrino, K. M.; Rodriguez, C. L.; Sleasman, T. A.; Spicer, G. L.; Steiner, N. E.; Vieth, A. P.; Wathen, J. J.; Wolfe, K. C.
abstract: Traumatic brain injury (TBI) is the leading cause of death and disability in people under 40 worldwide. There is an unmet need for detection and treatment of life-threatening TBI when computed tomography (CT) scanners and neurosurgeons are unavailable. We developed a new handheld frequency-domain multidetector infrared hemorrhage detection device. Using the new device, military pre-hospital medics required <4 minutes to detect life-threatening subdural hematoma in a sheep model. We developed a second device that allows non-neurosurgeons to safely create a burr hole and partially remove clotted subdural blood. In sheep, the treatment device reduced intracranial pressure within 20 minutes, and improved post-anesthesia blinded neurological outcomes. With human use adaptation, these devices could allow rapid detection and initial treatment of some life-threatening TBIs in challenging situations.

title: Intra-individual changes to peak alpha frequency map to pain perception following high frequency sensitisation of central nociceptive pathways: A test-retest reliability study
authors: Mugglestone, S.; Hughes, S. W.; Ganis, G.
abstract: Resting-state EEG can capture cortical dynamics relevant to sensitised pain states in the absence of ongoing nociceptive engagement. However, whilst the slowing of global oscillations is evident within various chronic pain conditions, the mechanistic specificity of PAF and -band power remains uncertain. Therefore, the present study assessed these features across two identical test-retest sessions in which HFS was applied to induce the development of SHA as characterised through 128 mN MPS. Crucially, changes in -band features post-HFS were investigated. Blind source separation was also applied to identify independent sensorimotor components relevant to nociception and assess their test-retest reliability. Results demonstrated good test-retest reliability for sensor-level data at baseline, with inter-individual changes in global PAF reflecting MPS post-HFS. However, no specific regional driver of this signal was evident. Alternatively, components identified through sensorimotor template matching revealed a significant influence of -band power on MPS both at baseline and post-HFS. However, only a small number of these components genuinely localised to pre- or post-central gyri, and test-retest reliability of -band power was poor. Together, these findings indicate that resting-state EEG may be useful for tracking changes in cortical -band oscillations alongside the development of pain sensitivity. However, methods of sensorimotor component identification evidenced limited agreement and global PAF slowing could not be linked to a specific electrode grouping.

title: Matching Corticospinal and Cortical Excitability along the motor cortex: TMS-EMG-EEG study
authors: Nazarova, M.; Higdon, M.; Rouste, J.; Mutanen, T. P.; Nikulin, V.; Ukharova, E.; Vaalto, S.; Ilmoniemi, R. J.; Lioumis, P.; Renvall, H.
abstract: There is still no consensus on how to choose intensities for transcranial magnetic stimulation (TMS). The resting motor threshold (RMT), the intensity needed to evoke muscle contractions in the contralateral limb muscles, is a robust muscle-specific index of corticospinal excitability. RMT from one of the hand muscles is commonly used as a reference for TMS neuromodulation interventions and TMS-electroencephalography (EEG) studies. However, it only provides an indirect measure of cortical excitability, and even for the primary motor cortex (M1), we do not understand how cortical and corticospinal excitability correspond to each other. Indeed, it remains unclear whether cortical responses to TMS follow similar location-dependent patterns along the M1, and whether subthreshold stimulation can reliably engage cortical circuits relevant to motor output. Combining TMS with electromyography (EMG) and EEG, TMS-EMG-EEG, enables simultaneous assessment of corticospinal and cortical excitability to answer these questions. We investigated how cortical excitability thresholds (CETs, measured with EEG), relate to corticospinal excitability thresholds (RMTs, measured with EMG) at the hand, arm, and leg hotspots along the M1 in 24 subjects. RMTs and CETs were strongly correlated, and both increased from hand to arm to leg. CETs were generally lower than RMTs, indicating that subthreshold stimulation was enough to evoke robust early TMS evoked potentials (TEPs). Within subjects, CETs differed from the corresponding RMTs at all three M1 hotspots, and this difference increased from hand to leg representations. The findings of the present study argue against using a default hand-muscle RMT to set cortical excitability dosage along the M1 and beyond. Online TMS-EEG can enable real-time dosing and could improve stimulation precision, efficiency, and generalizability, but the site-specific variability calls for adaptive control.
